1#א: "From benefit." The Shach wrote that it is explained in the Gemara that prohibitions involving benefit — such as basar b'chalav and the like — if they are a piece worthy of honor, prohibit their mixture also from benefit, even in [a ratio of] one thousand. However, it is permitted to sell them to a non-Jew, except for the value of the prohibition contained within them.
1#ב: "Leniently." For this stringency regarding a piece worthy of honor is only d'rabbanan. And see what was written at the beginning of siman 100.
2#א: "With milk." Because both of them have become one body — and the proof is that one receives lashes from the Torah if one ate approximately half an olive-measure of milk and half an olive-measure of meat. End of the words of the Taz.
2#ב: "Taste." For that which is absorbed is not worthy of honor. Based on this, the Torat Chatat wrote that a cheese curdled with treifah milk that subsequently became mixed in [with other cheese] is not a piece worthy of honor, since the prohibition within it is absorbed. The Bach was puzzled by this, for the Torat Chatat had ruled regarding non-Jewish cheese that a double doubt (sfek sfeika) does not help, since the prohibition is inherent to the cheese itself — and if so, here too he should have ruled that it is a piece worthy of honor. The Taz answered that there the discussion concerns cheese in which there is concern that non-kosher milk became mixed in and there was no nullification by a majority of kosher milk, and it teaches us that regarding a double doubt they were stringent, since the Sages prohibited it from the outset due to a d'oraisa doubt, and it is therefore called a certain treifah — for the first doubt is counted as certain. Whereas here the discussion is where there is a majority sufficient to nullify the prohibition, but you come to prohibit it due to the rule of a piece worthy of honor — regarding this I say that it is only an absorbed prohibition, and we do not apply the rule of a piece worthy of honor to it. He further wrote: nevertheless, it appears to me that we consider ordinary non-Jewish cheese as an absorbed prohibition, and it is nullified, and we do not say that it comes from treifah animal milk, since we follow the majority — see there. However, what he wrote at the end of his words — that if there is concern that the cheese was curdled with the stomach-lining of a neveilah, due to this it has the status of a piece worthy of honor, for there is a basar b'chalav prohibition here, end of his words — does not seem correct to me. For the reason we apply the rule of a piece worthy of honor to basar b'chalav is because each one of them is permitted on its own, and this logic does not apply to neveilah. Furthermore, it contradicts what the Mechaber wrote in siman 87, seif 11 — see there, and consider this carefully. It is possible, however, to press his words to mean that the prohibition of neveilah is a prohibition inherent to itself, and we apply a piece worthy of honor to it just as with basar b'chalav, which is also called a prohibition inherent to itself. And it is straightforward.
2#ג: "Peeling." The Shach wrote that this rule is only found regarding basar b'chalav, but regarding other prohibitions they were only prohibited due to absorbed taste, and it is obvious that they are not called a piece worthy of honor. However, there are decisors who hold that if one were to peel it, it would be a piece worthy of honor that is not nullified — see there.
3#א: "Worthy of honor." The Shach wrote that it is also not a counted item (davar shebeminyan), since it lacks such a significant degree of preparation. This is also the opinion of the Bach, unlike the Torat Chatat who wrote that it is a counted item. And see below, siman 110.
3#ב: "They removed it." Nevertheless, since at the time of the initial mixture it was nullified, it does not revert to being prohibited when stirred. Sefer Mitzvot Katan.
3#ג: "Whole." Even if its skin was removed.
3#ד: "In its feathers." The same law applies to a sheep in its skin, and the like.
3#ה: "Goose." The Torat Chatat wrote that goose legs whose skin has not been singed off them, as is the custom to do, are comparable to a chicken in its feathers. The Taz wrote that it implies that if the feathers were already removed but the innards had not yet been taken out and the belly had not been opened, it is still considered a piece worthy of honor and is not nullified. Maharshal wrote that the head of an animal is not considered worthy of honor, except for the head of a calf — and certainly the tongue of an ox is considered worthy of honor, for Abraham honored the angels with three tongues.
4#א: "The gizzard." The Taz wrote that for us, the outer membrane of the calf's gizzard is considered a piece worthy of honor.
4#ב: "Fat." The Shach wrote that Maharshal disagrees with this [and wrote that the outer membrane of the calf's gizzard is considered (a piece worthy of honor)]. Since these laws vary according to place and time, as will be seen below at the beginning of siman 110, I have been brief in this matter, and everything depends on the judgment of the decisor whether it is considered significant in that place or not; and if there is doubt, we are lenient. The Taz wrote that one may not be lenient regarding the skin of goose fat, even if it was cut into strips (called gribn), for even so it is called a piece worthy of honor. (And in Nekudat HaKesef he disagrees with this, for one does not honor a guest with one piece alone but only with many together, and if so, each individual piece by itself is not worthy of honor — see there.)
5#_: "Other." The Taz wrote in the name of Maharshal that the gizzard of a goose is considered a piece worthy of honor, and it implies that the gizzard of a chicken is not a piece worthy of honor. Maharshal further wrote that the sages of Krakow ruled that the goose breast meat called bilak — even though the skin was removed from it — is still worthy of honor, and he disagrees with this. The Taz's conclusion is that it is called a piece worthy of honor on the grounds that any piece currently worthy of honor, even though it was formerly even more significant, does not have its significance nullified. The Levush wrote that those goose livers that turned white due to the fat are certainly significant and are not nullified. The main point in this matter is that it depends on the place and time.
6#א: "Were crushed." The Torat Chatat wrote that it is implied in the Issur ve'Heter that the ruling that a beriah is nullified if it was crushed means that no significant item remained there; but if a piece worthy of honor remained, even though it was nullified due to the rule of beriah, nevertheless it is still considered significant and is not nullified due to the rule of a piece worthy of honor — and this is a correct reasoning, end of his words. (As is also written [there]: and correspondingly, what commonly falls off slightly through cooking is not considered crushing; but if it separated slightly from its body and from its spine or its head, that is considered crushing. And crushing is effective for any significant item, except for something that has a permitted aspect (davar she'yesh lo matirin) — see there.)
6#ב: "Of their own kind." The Taz explained: for example, a pot of vegetables in which a beriah was lost — everything is prohibited. And see below, siman 102, seif 1.
7#א: "Is permitted." The Issur ve'Heter wrote that this ruling speaks of when there are sixty [parts] of permitted food against the prohibited part; and what the Mechaber wrote, 'if it is of the prohibited type,' means that even the prohibited item is included within this doubt — namely, that perhaps it was cut.
7#ב: "We attribute it." Even though everywhere we follow the majority, nevertheless here we say that anything that has changed from its original state is attributed to the majority, and it is like the rule of 'anything that separates is attributed to the majority,' etc. Annotation of Shaarei Dura.
9#_: "Similar." The Taz wrote that it implies that they must also be equal in appearance. And even though regarding the fat of the gizzard the appearance of the fat alone suffices, here it is different — since it is possible to verify that they are also aligned in the cut, this is also required. The Issur ve'Heter wrote that nowadays, when we are not so expert in this, we cannot permit in such a case unless there is a large and obvious difference. The Bach wrote that he received this teaching from a certain sage: if fluid was found in the head of one sheep that would render it treifah, and it was not known from which sheep the head came, one should examine the spinal cord of the sheep — and whichever sheep has fluid in its head will have fluid in the cord extending from the brain to the spine, and we attribute the head to that sheep in order to permit the others. End of his words. The Taz concluded that in this matter it is not worthwhile to permit a doubtful treifah status on this basis, since it is not found in the Gemara or the decisors. And see above, siman 83.
